strengths: Addresses practical, well-motivated problem: zero-shot anomaly generation without fine-tuning or anomalous samples, valuable for real-world industrial deployment where defects are scarce and costly to curate.

Novel delta-denoising attribution mechanism that cleverly ties anomaly localization to diffusion model's own denoising dynamics by accumulating per-step latent discrepancies between normal and anomaly branches—more principled than prior attention-map-based approaches.

Comprehensive technical design combining normal-reference initialization, token-level prompt refinement (dual objectives for context alignment and semantic distillation), and spatial attention biasing. Each component is well-motivated and thoroughly ablated.

Thorough experimental evaluation with multiple metrics (IS, IC-LPIPS, AUROC, AP) and comprehensive baseline comparison (DRAEM, DFMGAN, AnomalyDiffusion, AnoGen, AnomalyAny) with fair zero-shot protocol and no test-set leakage.

Strong empirical results: achieves highest generation quality metrics (IS=2.03, IC-LPIPS=0.36) and consistent improvements over ZSAG baseline AnomalyAny in downstream detection (mean AUROC 84.7 vs 77.6).

Clear presentation with effective qualitative visualizations (Figure 3) demonstrating sharper boundaries and better realism than prior methods, plus comprehensive ablation studies (Table 3, Figures 4–5) validating design choices.
Truly training-free and cross-category generalizable, enabling immediate practical deployment for rapid data bootstrapping in production environments.
weaknesses: Inconsistent category-level downstream performance: several categories degrade vs. AnomalyAny (cable AUCp 82.2→76.2; capsule AUCi 59.4→54.9; leather APp 45.0→47.1 with much lower image-level scores). Pixel-level AP gains are often marginal, and paper acknowledges method struggles with complex/fine-grained defects, limiting claims of general superiority.

Limited component-level novelty: normal-reference initialization, prompt refinement, and spatial attention biasing are incremental adaptations of existing diffusion-editing techniques. Primary contribution is the combination rather than fundamental methodological innovation.

Critical evaluation gaps: (1) Mask quality lacks direct quantitative evaluation (no F1/IoU vs. ground truth masks, only indirect downstream detection); (2) computational cost completely absent (two 100-step diffusion branches is expensive; no inference time comparison); (3) cross-dataset generalization missing from main paper—results on 'other datasets' relegated to appendix; (4) threshold choices (τmid=0.6, τfinal=0.35) lack sensitivity analysis and justification for split at tmid.

Prompt engineering dependence: success requires selecting appropriate anomaly descriptors per defect type; no systematic guidelines or sensitivity study provided. Real-world deployment requires domain expertise to determine suitable prompts for novel defect types.

External dependencies and failure modes: relies on SAM (Segment Anything Model) for foreground mask Mfg; impact of SAM failure on robustness not discussed. Hyperparameter choices (γ=0.3, T=100) lack justification or ablation.

Insufficient failure analysis: no systematic investigation of which defect categories/types fail systematically (e.g., do structural vs. surface defects behave differently?). Category-dependent variance (Table 2) suggests limited robustness but no diagnosis provided.

Acknowledged but unresolved limitations: controllability 'remains limited' per authors; evaluation protocols 'are limited and may require MLLM-based assessment'; generated anomalies are primarily 'structural or surface-level' while 'abstract or logical defects remain challenging.'

Reproducibility concerns: code not yet available; critical hyperparameters (T, γ, thresholds) lack ablation studies or principled selection; tied to Stable Diffusion v1.5 specifics, generalization to newer checkpoints unclear.

Notation and clarity: ⊙ operator used ambiguously for both element-wise and mask-guided operations; 'clean()' operation in Algorithm 1 undefined; relationship between masks (Mfg, Mmid, M) not sufficiently explicit.

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing practical scarcity of anomalous data with clear deployment motivation
Novel core concept (delta-denoising attribution) with intuitive design that leverages synchronized diffusion branches without supervision
Comprehensive experimental validation on two benchmarks (MVTec AD, VisA) with multiple evaluation perspectives and strong baselines
Each method component is well-justified with convincing ablations demonstrating necessity and contribution
Achieves competitive results with FSAG methods on some categories (89.7% AUCi with FLUX); outperforms some ZSAG baselines
Model-agnostic framework demonstrating transferability from Stable Diffusion v1.5 to FLUX.1-dev
Practical efficiency considerations with favorable runtime/memory compared to AnomalyAny
Refreshing transparency about evaluation protocol limitations and method constraints (acknowledged in Appendix D)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: individual components (latent inpainting, prompt refinement, attention biasing) are known; primary contribution is their combination for ZSAG
Acknowledged but consequential evaluation limitations: IC-LPIPS metrics fundamentally misaligned for ZSAG since they assume real anomaly anchors that zero-shot methods don't observe
Performance remains category-dependent with notable variance (cable: 70.9% AUCi; screw: 73.3% with only 4.7% APp), suggesting method brittleness
Threshold sensitivity (Table 6: range 78.8%–88.6% AUCi across T1 values) contradicts 'zero-shot' claim; universal defaults require empirical tuning
Hyperparameter choices lack justification (γ=0.3, β=4, η=4, λ=0.5); why L2 norm specifically in Eq. 8? No ablation on distance metrics
Two-threshold strategy (tmid vs. final) and accumulator reset at mid-denoising appear empirically motivated without principled justification
Marginal improvements over existing ZSAG baselines (e.g., Table 1: 2.05 vs. 2.02 IS; differences within noise given evaluation concerns)
Constrained scope: limited to structural/surface defects, prompt-based anomaly specification, SAM dependency despite claimed independence
Insufficient analysis: no feature-space comparison of synthesized vs. real anomaly distributions; limited failure mode discussion
Reproducibility concerns: code unavailable at review; many design decisions lack clear justification
